newsitem.title: Canada: Minor issues delay Ford Canada, union deal.
newsitem.headline: Minor issues delay Ford Canada, union deal.

text.p: The Canadian Auto Workers said contract talks with Ford Motor Co. of Canada Ltd. have stalled over minor issues and would likely go down to the wire despite earlier hopes a deal could be reached well ahead of a Wednesday 7 P.M. EST strike deadline.
CAW President Buzz Hargrove said the two sides had made little progress on several local and administrative sticking points despite having settled the pattern issues on Monday.

"I am frustrated, disappointed. I would have thought we could have gone out tonight for a bottle of wine, dinner, to celebrate this thing but it doesn't look like that's going to happen," said Hargrove.
The main roadblock to a deal is a conflict over the scheduling of paid leave, which Hargrove said Ford bargainers are calling a "showstopper."
The union said workers should be able to book the leave according to seniority, as vacations are scheduled, but Ford wants to use a computer-generated schedule for the leave.

Ford spokesman Jim Hartford said Ford wants to be held to the same standards as Chrysler Corp. and General Motors Corp. The pattern deal reached by the CAW with Chrysler and GM allows the schedule to be computer generated.
Hargrove said the culture at Ford has always allowed for more scheduling flexibility, and he complained that Ford chief negotiator Donald McKenzie was holding up a deal over administrative details.
"These issues shouldn't be something that will hold it up," said Hargrove. "These issues will come together, the only question is when he decides to do it."
But Hartford said the sticking points, which also include local issues like working conditions at specific plants, cannot be settled easily.

"(The issues) are small, some of them, and some of them may appear almost insignificant, but they are important to the local people, and certainly important to the local management as well, so they can be sticking," said Hartford.
A frustrated Hargrove, who had been sounding conciliatory since Monday, warned the delays could result in a strike.
"Certainly given the lengthy list we have today and given the importance of some of the issues, there's enough here to put this thing in the ditch if we cannot find a resolution."
A source close to the union, however, said the talks would go down to the wire simply because negotiators on both sides needed to show their constituents they had fought to the end.
Hargrove said union negotiators, who represent about 11,700 Ford workers, would work through the night ahead of a 9 A.M. EST (1400 GMT) Wednesday caucus meeting.

The pattern deal offers the union protection from outsourcing, or contracting out jobs, ensures minimum health and safety and employment standards and gives workers improved benefits and a 10.2 percent wage and cost of living increase over three years.
Ford Canada is a wholly owned unit of Ford Motor Co.
